scenario: A 45-year-old previously healthy female being treated for pyelonephritis with IV ceftriaxone develops stridor, respiratory distress, angioedema, and a widespread urticarial rash consistent with anaphylaxis. The scenario focuses on anaphylaxis management, difficult airway planning, failed intubation, and surgical cricothyrotomy.

messages.speaker: clinician
messages.content: I'm putting a tight-fitting oxygen mask on your face right now — your oxygen level is at 88%, which is dangerously low, so this is the first thing we need to fix. While we get this on you, can you tell me what brought you in today?

messages.speaker: nurse
messages.content: NRB mask on at 90% FiO2.

patient_emotion.notes: [clinician: I'm putting a tight-fitting oxygen mask on your face right now — your oxygen level is at 88%, which is dangerously low, so this is the first thing we need to fix. While we get this on you, can you tell me what brought you in today?] FEAR: not at all → low. The clinician directly discloses a serious, newly revealed abnormality — an oxygen saturation of 88% described as 'dangerously low.' Per the clinical threat escalation rule, this is unambiguously bad news and must raise fear at least one level. Starting from 'not at all,' the one-level-per-utterance cap and the absence of an imminent-death framing keep this at 'low' rather than 'high.' The fact that the clinician immediately frames it as 'the first thing we need to fix' (a plan) buffers the magnitude but cannot cancel the rise. OVERWHELM: not at all → low. The patient is simultaneously experiencing an urgent physical intervention (mask placed on her face), receiving alarming clinical information (dangerous O2 stat), and being asked a question requiring recall and verbal response. This constitutes multiple demands hitting at once — enough to lift overwhelm one level from absent to low. SADNESS: remains not at all — no loss, damage, or hopeless prognosis is conveyed. SHAME: remains not at all — no judgment, blame, or stigmatizing content is present.

messages.speaker: patient
messages.content: I came in for flank pain and fever — but something's wrong, I can't breathe right, my throat feels tight, my lips and tongue are swelling up, I've got hives all over, I feel dizzy and like I'm going to pass out, and I've been nauseated and throwing up. I also have pain when I urinate.

messages.speaker: clinician
messages.content: Epinephrine 0.5 mg IM, 1:1000, stat — this is anaphylaxis.

messages.speaker: nurse
messages.content: Epinephrine 0.5 mg IM 1:1000 given.

messages.speaker: clinician
messages.content: Before this started — any known allergies, or did you eat, take, or get exposed to anything new, including any medications?

messages.speaker: nurse
messages.content: Methylprednisolone 125 mg IV administered.

patient_emotion.notes: [clinician: Before this started — any known allergies, or did you eat, take, or get exposed to anything new, including any medications?] No emotions change this tick. This is a neutral, non-judgmental history-gathering question with no new clinical disclosure. Fear stays low: no new bad news, worsening finding, or threat escalation is delivered — the team is simply trying to identify the trigger, which does not itself constitute a threat escalation for the patient. Overwhelm stays low: it is a single compound question and, while the rules note questions are not soothing, there is insufficient load here to push low→high; the patient has already fielded complex exchanges and this asks only for a familiar category of personal history. Sadness stays not at all: no loss, damage, or irreversible outcome is implied. Shame stays not at all: the question includes 'any medications' which can carry a mild exposure risk, but the framing is completely neutral and investigative with no accusatory or judgmental cue — standard anaphylaxis workup does not itself trigger shame.

messages.speaker: patient
messages.content: No known allergies. I've been taking nitrofurantoin — started it recently.

messages.speaker: clinician
messages.content: Diphenhydramine 50 mg IV now — anaphylaxis adjunct.

messages.speaker: nurse
messages.content: Diphenhydramine 50 mg IV administered.

messages.speaker: clinician
messages.content: 1 liter normal saline wide open IV — she's still tachycardic at 140, distributive shock from the anaphylaxis.

messages.speaker: clinician
messages.content: Get RSI setup at the bedside now — sat's 89% on NRB with angioedema and throat tightness, this airway is closing.

messages.speaker: nurse
messages.content: Airway setup in progress. BVM, suction, and intubation equipment at bedside. Ready when you are.

messages.speaker: clinician
messages.content: Your oxygen is at 86% and your airway is swelling shut from the allergic reaction — it's not responding enough to the medications. I need to put a breathing tube in right now. I'm going to give you something to put you to sleep first, then place the tube. We're doing this now.

messages.speaker: nurse
messages.content: RSI meds in, attempting intubation now.

messages.speaker: clinician
messages.content: Tube didn't go — sat's 76%, we're going surgical. Open the cric kit now, I'm doing a scalpel cricothyrotomy.

messages.speaker: nurse
messages.content: Scalpel-finger-bougie cricothyrotomy at the cricothyroid membrane — proceeding.

messages.speaker: clinician
messages.content: Start epinephrine infusion, 0.1 mcg/kg/min IV, titrate up — BP is 92/56, she's not coming out of shock on the IM dose alone.

messages.speaker: nurse
messages.content: Epinephrine infusion running at 0.1–0.5 mcg/kg/min IV. Monitoring for response.

messages.speaker: clinician
messages.content: Start propofol infusion, 5 mcg/kg/min IV, titrate up — she needs to stay down on the vent.

messages.speaker: clinician
messages.content: Portable CXR stat — need to confirm cric tube position.

messages.speaker: clinician
messages.content: Push 1L normal saline IV bolus now — BP is still 96/59 on epi, she needs volume.

messages.speaker: nurse
messages.content: 1000 mL normal saline bolus is running.

messages.speaker: clinician
messages.content: Get that CXR now — sat is only 94% on 100% FiO2, I need to confirm cric tube position and rule out pneumothorax.

errors: Diagnostic test_name 'Chest X-ray' is already pending; duplicate diagnostic_order is not allowed.

messages.speaker: nurse
messages.content: CXR back — normal chest radiograph. No pneumothorax. BP 99/60, HR 160, sat 93% on 100% FiO2.

messages.speaker: clinician
messages.content: Give albuterol 2.5mg nebulized via ETT — sats are 93% on 100% FiO2 with a normal CXR, bronchospasm is the issue.

messages.speaker: nurse
messages.content: Albuterol 2.5 mg nebulized via ETT administered.

messages.speaker: clinician
messages.content: 12-lead ECG now — HR is 168 and BP is 96/58, I need to confirm the rhythm and rule out ischemia.
